questions.s: Which definition of economics describes it as the science of human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means that have alternative uses?
questions.e: Robbins built his definition on unlimited ends, scarce means and alternative uses of those means. Marshall's definition stresses material welfare, and Smith's calls economics the science of wealth.

questions.s: The basic economic problem that every society faces arises because
o: wants are unlimited while resources are scarce
governments collect too much in taxes
money and income are unevenly shared among people
prices tend to rise over time
questions.e: Scarcity of resources relative to unlimited wants forces every society to choose what, how and for whom to produce. Unequal incomes and inflation are problems in some economies, but they are not the root of the basic problem.

questions.s: Bilal can spend his Saturday either working at a shop for Rs 2,000 or attending a coaching class. He chooses the class. What is the opportunity cost of the class?
o: Nothing, as he chose the class freely
The fee he pays for the class
The value of the knowledge he gains
questions.e: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone, here the Rs 2,000 wage. The knowledge gained is the benefit of the class, not its cost.

questions.s: A production possibility curve that is concave (bowed outward) from the origin shows that
o: opportunity cost falls as more of one good is produced
opportunity cost rises as more of one good is produced
opportunity cost stays constant along the curve
questions.e: Resources are not equally suited to both goods, so each extra unit of one good costs more and more of the other: increasing opportunity cost gives the outward bow. A straight-line PPC would show constant cost.

questions.s: An economy is producing at a point inside its production possibility curve. This means that
o: the economy is producing beyond its full productive capacity
some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
questions.e: Points on the curve use all resources fully and efficiently; a point inside it means output could rise without giving anything up. Points outside the curve are unattainable with current resources.

questions.s: An outward shift of the whole production possibility curve is most likely caused by
o: a fall in the price of one good
a move from unemployment to full employment
questions.e: Better technology or more resources increase the economy's capacity to produce both goods, shifting the curve outward. Reducing unemployment moves the economy from inside the curve to the curve, not the curve itself.

questions.s: Which branch of economics studies the behaviour of an individual firm or household?
questions.e: Microeconomics studies individual units such as a consumer, firm or industry. Macroeconomics deals with aggregates such as national income and the general price level.

questions.s: Which statement is a normative statement?
o: Higher interest rates can reduce borrowing by firms and households
Pakistan imports some of its crude oil
A rise in price reduces the quantity demanded
The government ought to reduce the tax on wheat
questions.e: A normative statement is a value judgement about what ought to be and cannot be tested by facts. The others are positive statements that can be checked against evidence.

questions.s: According to the law of demand, other things remaining the same,
o: quantity demanded rises when income rises
quantity demanded falls when price rises
questions.e: The law of demand states an inverse relation between a good's own price and the quantity demanded, ceteris paribus. The income effect describes a shift of demand, not the law of demand itself.

questions.s: The price of tea rises. Which of the following is most likely to happen in the market for sugar, a good used with tea?
o: Demand for sugar falls and its curve shifts left
The supply curve of sugar shifts right
Demand for sugar rises and its curve shifts right
Quantity of sugar demanded rises along its curve
questions.e: Tea and sugar are complements: dearer tea means less tea drunk and so less sugar wanted at every price, shifting sugar's demand curve left. A movement along the curve would need a change in sugar's own price.

questions.s: A movement along a demand curve, rather than a shift of the curve, is caused by a change in
o: the price of the good itself
the price of a substitute good
questions.e: Only a change in the good's own price moves the consumer along a given demand curve. Income, prices of related goods and tastes are the conditions of demand: they shift the whole curve.

questions.s: Ayesha's income rises and she buys less of a cheap brand of cooking oil. For her, this oil is
o: a Giffen good with an upward demand curve
questions.e: An inferior good is one whose demand falls as income rises, because buyers switch to better alternatives. A normal good's demand rises with income, and a Giffen good is a rare inferior good whose demand rises with its own price.

questions.s: A Giffen good is an exception to the law of demand because, when its price rises,
o: its supply rises at the same time
buyers expect its price to rise even further in the coming months
it is bought to show off wealth
a strong negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect
questions.e: For a staple inferior good taking a large share of a poor household's budget, a price rise cuts real income so much that the family buys more of the staple and less of better food. Buying to show off wealth describes a Veblen good, a different exception.

questions.s: Expensive diamonds being bought more when their price rises, because they signal status, is an example of
questions.e: Veblen goods are demanded partly for their high price as a status symbol, so demand can rise with price. A Giffen good is an inferior staple, not a luxury.

questions.s: Which of the following shifts the supply curve of wheat to the right?
o: A new tax on each bag of wheat
A rise in the price of wheat
A fall in the price of fertiliser
A rise in consumers' incomes and spending on bread
questions.e: Cheaper inputs lower the cost of production, so farmers offer more wheat at every price. A rise in wheat's own price causes a movement along the supply curve, and a tax per unit shifts supply left.

questions.s: The law of supply states that, other things being equal,
o: quantity supplied rises as price rises
quantity supplied rises as price falls
questions.e: Higher prices make production more profitable and draw in more output, so price and quantity supplied move in the same direction. The equality of supply and demand describes equilibrium, not the law of supply.

questions.s: In a market, the quantity demanded is greater than the quantity supplied at the current price. What will happen next if the market is free?
o: Price will rise until the shortage disappears
Price will fall until the excess supply disappears
Supply curve will shift to the left
questions.e: Excess demand is a shortage: buyers compete for scarce goods and bid the price up, which lowers quantity demanded and raises quantity supplied until they are equal. A surplus would push the price down instead.

questions.s: The demand for a good is Qd = 100 − 4P and the supply is Qs = 20 + 4P. What is the equilibrium price?
questions.e: Set 100 − 4P = 20 + 4P, so 80 = 8P and P = 10. The equilibrium quantity is 100 − 40 = 60 units. Rs 20 comes from dividing 80 by 4 instead of 8.

questions.s: Demand for a good is Qd = 120 − 2P and supply is Qs = 3P − 30. If the government fixes a maximum price of Rs 25, the market will have
o: neither a shortage nor a surplus
questions.e: Equilibrium is where 120 − 2P = 3P − 30, so P = 30. The ceiling of Rs 25 is below it: Qd = 120 − 50 = 70 and Qs = 75 − 30 = 45, a shortage of 70 − 45 = 25 units. 45 is the quantity supplied, not the gap.

questions.s: A government sets a minimum support price for wheat above the equilibrium price. The most likely result is
o: a fall in the price of wheat
questions.e: A price floor above equilibrium makes farmers offer more and buyers take less, leaving unsold wheat. A floor set below equilibrium would have no effect, and a ceiling below equilibrium causes shortages.

questions.s: A fall in the price of petrol and, at the same time, a large rise in the number of car buyers would have what effect on the market for cars?
o: Demand for cars falls, lowering price and quantity
Only the quantity of cars changes, not price
Demand for cars rises, raising price and quantity
Supply of cars rises, lowering their price
questions.e: Petrol is a complement to cars, so cheaper petrol raises car demand, and more buyers raise it further. Both factors shift the demand curve right, so with unchanged supply both price and quantity of cars rise.

questions.s: Price elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of
o: quantity demanded to a change in consumers' money income
quantity demanded to a change in the good's price
supply to a change in the good's price
price to a change in quantity supplied
questions.e: PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price. Responsiveness of demand to income is income elasticity, and that of supply to price is elasticity of supply.

questions.s: The price of a packet of biscuits rises from Rs 50 to Rs 60 and the quantity demanded falls from 400 to 300 packets. Using the original values, what is the price elasticity of demand (in absolute terms)?
questions.e: % change in quantity = 100 ÷ 400 = 25 %; % change in price = 10 ÷ 50 = 20 %. PED = 25 ÷ 20 = 1.25. 0.8 is the inverse ratio, price change over quantity change.

questions.s: When the price of a good falls by 10 %, its quantity demanded rises by 4 %. The demand for this good is
questions.e: PED = 4 % ÷ 10 % = 0.4, which is less than 1, so demand is inelastic. 2.5 comes from dividing the price change by the quantity change.

questions.s: Demand for a good is price elastic. If its seller lowers the price, total revenue will
questions.e: With elastic demand the percentage rise in quantity exceeds the percentage fall in price, so price × quantity rises. Revenue would fall only if demand were inelastic.

questions.s: A shopkeeper raises the price of salt and finds that his total revenue from salt rises. This shows that the demand for salt is
questions.e: Under the total outlay method, revenue moving in the same direction as price means demand is inelastic: quantity falls proportionately less than price rises. Salt has few substitutes and takes a small share of income.

questions.s: When the price of a good falls from Rs 20 to Rs 15, total expenditure on it stays at Rs 3,000. The price elasticity of demand over this range is
questions.e: Unchanged total expenditure after a price change is the sign of unitary elasticity in the total outlay method. Quantity rose from 150 to 200 exactly offsetting the lower price. Zero elasticity would mean quantity did not change at all, so spending would have fallen.

questions.s: Which good is likely to have the most price-elastic demand?
o: One particular brand of soft drink
questions.e: A single brand has many close substitutes, so buyers switch when its price rises. Salt, essential medicine and household electricity are necessities with few substitutes, so their demand is inelastic.

questions.s: Which factor makes the demand for a good more price inelastic?
o: Buyers have a long time to adjust
It takes a very small share of income
It is a luxury rather than a necessity
questions.e: When spending on a good is a tiny part of the budget, a price change hardly matters to buyers, so demand is inelastic. More substitutes, luxury status and longer time to adjust all make demand more elastic.

questions.s: A consumer's income rises from Rs 40,000 to Rs 50,000 and her demand for fruit rises from 20 kg to 30 kg a month. Her income elasticity of demand for fruit is
questions.e: % change in quantity = 10 ÷ 20 = 50 %; % change in income = 10,000 ÷ 40,000 = 25 %. YED = 50 ÷ 25 = 2. A positive value above 1 marks fruit as a luxury for her; 0.5 inverts the ratio.

questions.s: The income elasticity of demand for a good is negative. The good is
questions.e: Negative income elasticity means demand falls as income rises, the definition of an inferior good. Necessities have income elasticity between 0 and 1, and luxuries above 1.

questions.s: The cross elasticity of demand between two goods is positive. The two goods are
questions.e: A rise in the price of one good raising demand for the other gives a positive cross elasticity, the mark of substitutes such as tea and coffee. Complements have negative cross elasticity, and unrelated goods have zero.

questions.s: The price of good X rises by 20 % and the quantity demanded of good Y falls by 10 %. What is the cross elasticity of demand for Y with respect to the price of X, and how are the goods related?
questions.e: Cross elasticity = % change in Qy ÷ % change in Px = −10 ÷ 20 = −0.5. The negative sign shows that dearer X reduces demand for Y, so they are used together. −2 comes from dividing the wrong way round.

questions.s: A vertical supply curve shows that the elasticity of supply is
questions.e: A vertical supply curve means the same quantity is offered whatever the price, so quantity does not respond at all: elasticity is zero. Fresh fish at the end of a day's market is a common example.

questions.s: The price of a good rises from Rs 80 to Rs 100 and the quantity supplied rises from 500 to 600 units. Using the original values, the elasticity of supply is
questions.e: % change in quantity supplied = 100 ÷ 500 = 20 %; % change in price = 20 ÷ 80 = 25 %. Es = 20 ÷ 25 = 0.8, so supply is inelastic. 1.25 is the inverse ratio.

questions.s: Supply of most farm crops is relatively inelastic in the short run mainly because
o: farmers do not respond to prices
output cannot be raised until the next harvest
demand for food is always elastic
crops are sold only by the government
questions.e: Once a crop is sown, the quantity cannot be increased quickly; supply becomes more elastic over a longer period as farmers adjust what they plant. Farmers do respond to prices, but only with a time lag.

questions.s: In economics, utility means
o: the satisfaction a consumer gets from a good
the price a consumer pays for a good
the usefulness of a good to society
the cost of producing a good
questions.e: Utility is the want-satisfying power of a good as felt by a consumer; it is subjective and need not be morally useful. A cigarette has utility for a smoker even though it harms health.

questions.s: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that as a consumer takes more units of a good,
o: the price of the good falls
total satisfaction falls from the first unit
the extra satisfaction from each unit rises
the extra satisfaction from each unit falls
questions.e: Each additional unit adds less to total utility than the one before, because the want is gradually satisfied. Total utility still rises as long as marginal utility is positive.

questions.s: Hamza's total utility from eating 1, 2, 3 and 4 samosas is 20, 35, 45 and 50 utils respectively. What is the marginal utility of the third samosa?
questions.e: MU of the third unit = TU(3) − TU(2) = 45 − 35 = 10 utils. 45 is the total utility of three samosas, and 15 is the MU of the second one.

questions.s: When marginal utility from a good is zero, total utility is
questions.e: Total utility rises while MU is positive, stops rising when MU is zero and falls once MU turns negative. So zero MU marks the point of maximum total utility, the point of satiety.

questions.s: A consumer spends her income on goods X and Y. MU of X is 30 utils and its price is Rs 10; MU of Y is 40 utils and its price is Rs 20. To increase total utility she should
o: buy more Y and less X
buy more X and less Y
questions.e: MUx ÷ Px = 30 ÷ 10 = 3 utils per rupee, and MUy ÷ Py = 40 ÷ 20 = 2. A rupee spent on X gives more satisfaction, so she should shift spending to X until the ratios are equal. Comparing MU alone wrongly points to Y.

questions.s: The law of equi-marginal utility says that a consumer gets maximum satisfaction from a given income when
o: MU per rupee is equal across all goods bought
the same amount is spent on each good
MU is equal for every good bought
total utility from each good is equal
questions.e: Consumer equilibrium needs MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py = … for all goods, with all income spent. Equal MU without dividing by price ignores that goods cost different amounts.

questions.s: Consumer surplus is the difference between
o: what a consumer is willing to pay and what she actually pays
a consumer's income and her spending
the market price of a good and the seller's cost of production
questions.e: Consumer surplus measures the extra benefit a buyer gets when the market price is below the most she would pay. The gap between price and cost relates to the producer's profit, not the consumer.

questions.s: A consumer is willing to pay Rs 50, Rs 40, Rs 30 and Rs 20 for the first, second, third and fourth units of a good. If the market price is Rs 20 and he buys 4 units, his total consumer surplus is
questions.e: Surplus on each unit = willingness to pay − 20, giving 30 + 20 + 10 + 0 = Rs 60. Rs 140 is the total he is willing to pay, and Rs 80 is what he actually spends.

questions.s: Indifference curves are normally convex to the origin because of
o: a constant marginal rate of substitution
increasing marginal utility of both goods
a rise in the consumer's income
a diminishing marginal rate of substitution
questions.e: As the consumer has more of X and less of Y, she gives up fewer and fewer units of Y for each extra unit of X; this falling MRS bends the curve towards the origin. A constant MRS would give a straight line, as with perfect substitutes.

questions.s: A consumer is in equilibrium on an indifference map at the point where
o: the budget line touches the highest indifference curve
the budget line cuts the lowest indifference curve
two indifference curves cross each other
the budget line meets the vertical axis
questions.e: With a given income and prices, the best affordable combination is where the budget line is tangent to the highest reachable indifference curve, so MRS equals the price ratio. Indifference curves never cross.

questions.s: A consumer has Rs 600 to spend on good X at Rs 30 each and good Y at Rs 20 each. If she buys 10 units of X, how many units of Y can she buy with the rest?
questions.e: Spending on X = 10 × 30 = Rs 300, leaving 600 − 300 = Rs 300 for Y. At Rs 20 each, she can buy 300 ÷ 20 = 15 units. 30 is the maximum Y if she bought no X.

questions.s: A demand schedule is a
o: table showing a firm's costs at each output
list of goods a household buys each month
graph showing quantities supplied at different prices
table showing quantities demanded at different prices
questions.e: A demand schedule lists the price and the matching quantity demanded; plotting it gives the demand curve. A supply schedule does the same for quantities offered by sellers.

questions.s: Market demand for a good is obtained by
o: averaging the demand of all buyers
multiplying price by the quantity demanded
adding the quantities demanded by all buyers at each price
adding the prices that all buyers are willing to pay for one unit
questions.e: Market demand is the horizontal sum of individual demand curves: at each price, add up what every buyer wants. Price × quantity gives expenditure, not market demand.

questions.s: Using the midpoint (arc) method, what is the price elasticity of demand when price rises from Rs 40 to Rs 60 and quantity demanded falls from 120 to 80 units?
questions.e: Change in Q = 40 on an average of 100, so 40 %; change in P = 20 on an average of 50, so 40 %. PED = 40 ÷ 40 = 1. Using the starting values instead gives 33.3 % ÷ 50 % ≈ 0.67, which is why the midpoint method is used for large changes.

questions.s: On a straight-line downward-sloping demand curve, price elasticity of demand at the midpoint of the line is
o: the same as at every other point
questions.e: Along a straight-line demand curve the slope is constant but elasticity is not: it is above 1 on the upper half, 1 at the midpoint and below 1 on the lower half. Equal slope does not mean equal elasticity.

questions.s: The phrase ceteris paribus, used when stating economic laws, means
o: only at the equilibrium market price
questions.e: Laws such as the law of demand hold only if factors other than the one studied, such as income and tastes, do not change. It does not refer to time periods or market forms.

questions.s: Buyers expect the price of cement to rise sharply next month. The likely effect on the market for cement today is
o: demand falls and the demand curve shifts left
a movement down along the demand curve
supply rises and the supply curve shifts right
demand rises and the demand curve shifts right
questions.e: Expecting higher future prices, buyers bring purchases forward, so demand at every current price increases. A movement along the curve would need a change in today's price, not in expectations.

questions.s: The demand for bricks that comes from the demand for new houses is an example of
questions.e: Derived demand is demand for a good or factor because it helps produce something else that people want. Composite demand is when one good has several different uses, such as milk for butter and for tea.

questions.s: The government places a tax of Rs 10 per unit on a good whose demand is perfectly inelastic. Who bears the tax?
o: The sellers bear all of it
Buyers and sellers share it equally
The buyers bear all of it
questions.e: With perfectly inelastic demand, buyers take the same quantity whatever the price, so sellers can pass the whole tax on and price rises by the full Rs 10. If demand were perfectly elastic, sellers would bear it all.

questions.s: The cardinal approach to utility assumes that utility
o: is the same for every consumer
can be measured in numbers called utils
is the same as the market price
can only be ranked in order of preference, not measured
questions.e: Marshall's cardinal approach treats utility as measurable, so marginal utility can be stated as a number of utils. The ordinal, indifference curve approach only ranks combinations as preferred or indifferent.

questions.s: Demand for a good is Qd = 200 − 5P and supply is Qs = 50 + 10P. What is the equilibrium quantity?
questions.e: Set 200 − 5P = 50 + 10P, so 150 = 15P and P = 10. Then Q = 200 − 50 = 150 units, and supply gives the same 50 + 100 = 150. 10 is the equilibrium price, not quantity.

questions.s: Which of these is a determinant of supply rather than of demand?
o: The state of technology used by firms
questions.e: Technology changes the cost of production, so it shifts the supply curve. Tastes, population and income affect how much buyers want, so they shift demand.

questions.s: Wheat and straw are produced together, so they are in joint supply. If demand for wheat rises, the likely effect in the straw market is
o: demand for straw rises and its price rises
no change, as straw is a separate good
supply of straw falls and its price rises
supply of straw rises and its price falls
questions.e: Growing more wheat automatically produces more straw, so the supply of straw shifts right and, with unchanged demand, its price falls. Treating straw as unrelated misses the link in production.

questions.s: At an output where price elasticity of demand equals one, a seller's total revenue is
questions.e: While demand is elastic, a price cut raises revenue; once it becomes inelastic, a price cut lowers revenue. Revenue therefore peaks where elasticity is exactly one.

questions.s: An increase in demand, shown by a rightward shift of the demand curve, with supply unchanged leads to
o: a lower price and a larger quantity
a higher price and a smaller quantity
a higher price and a larger quantity
a lower price and a smaller quantity
questions.e: At the old price there is now a shortage, so price rises and sellers move up the supply curve to offer more. A fall in price with a larger quantity is the result of an increase in supply.

questions.s: Which change would cause a contraction (fall in quantity) along the supply curve of mangoes?
o: A pest attack on mango orchards
A rise in the wages of farm workers
A new tax on each crate of mangoes
A fall in the market price of mangoes
questions.e: Only a change in the good's own price moves sellers along the supply curve; a lower price leads them to offer less. Pests, higher wages and a per-unit tax raise costs or cut output at every price, shifting the curve left.

questions.s: If both demand and supply of a good increase by the same amount, the equilibrium
o: price rises while quantity stays the same
quantity rises while price stays about the same
questions.e: A rightward shift of demand raises price and quantity; a rightward shift of supply lowers price and raises quantity. Equal shifts cancel the price effects but reinforce the rise in quantity.

questions.s: A horizontal straight-line demand curve shows demand that is
questions.e: A horizontal demand curve means buyers will take any quantity at one price but none above it: elasticity is infinite. A vertical curve shows perfectly inelastic demand.

questions.s: Sana is willing to pay Rs 1,500 for a school bag but buys it for Rs 1,200. Her consumer surplus is
questions.e: Consumer surplus = willingness to pay − price paid = 1,500 − 1,200 = Rs 300. Rs 1,200 is just the price she paid.

questions.s: An indifference curve shows combinations of two goods that give a consumer
o: the same quantity of each good
questions.e: Every point on one indifference curve gives equal satisfaction, so the consumer is indifferent between them. Combinations costing the same lie on a budget line, not an indifference curve.

questions.s: Goods that are freely available in nature and have no price, such as air, are called
questions.e: Free goods are not scarce, so no sacrifice is needed to obtain them and they carry no price. Economic goods are scarce and command a price; public goods are non-rival and non-excludable but cost resources to provide.

questions.s: Which factor of production organises the other factors and bears the risk of the business?
questions.e: The entrepreneur combines land, labour and capital and bears the uncertainty of business, earning profit as the reward. Labour earns wages, capital interest and land rent.

questions.s: The reward for land as a factor of production is called
questions.e: Each factor has its own reward: land earns rent, labour wages, capital interest and the entrepreneur profit.

questions.s: In economics, which of the following counts as capital?
o: A tractor owned by a farmer
Money kept in a savings account at home
The skill of a trained mechanic
questions.e: Capital is man-made wealth used to produce further goods, such as machines and tools. Soil is land, a mechanic's skill is part of labour (human capital in a wider sense), and idle money is not a physical factor of production.

questions.s: Which feature belongs to land as a factor of production?
o: It is fully mobile between places
Its supply rises easily with price
questions.e: Land, meaning all natural resources, is a gift of nature with a fixed total supply and no geographical mobility. Capital, not land, is man-made.

questions.s: One major advantage of the division of labour is that
o: workers gain speed and skill by repeating one task
the risk of unemployment falls for every worker in the firm
work becomes more interesting and varied
each worker learns to make the whole product
questions.e: Specialising in one small task builds skill, saves time between tasks and encourages the use of machines. Its drawbacks include monotony and the risk of unemployment if that one task disappears.

questions.s: The law of diminishing returns applies when
o: the price of output keeps falling
a firm uses only one factor of production
all factors are increased together in the same proportion
more of one variable factor is added to fixed factors
questions.e: Diminishing returns is a short-run law: with at least one factor fixed, adding more units of the variable factor eventually brings smaller additions to output. Increasing all factors together concerns returns to scale.

questions.s: A farmer adds workers to a fixed plot of land. Total product with 1, 2, 3 and 4 workers is 10, 24, 33 and 38 tonnes. What is the marginal product of the third worker?
questions.e: MP of the third worker = TP(3) − TP(2) = 33 − 24 = 9 tonnes. 11 is the average product of three workers, and 14 is the MP of the second worker.

questions.s: A factory with 5 workers produces 60 chairs a week. What is the average product of labour?
questions.e: AP = total product ÷ number of workers = 60 ÷ 5 = 12 chairs. Marginal product would need the change in output from adding one worker, which is not given.

questions.s: When total product is at its maximum, marginal product is
questions.e: TP rises while MP is positive and starts to fall when MP becomes negative, so at the peak of TP the MP is zero. MP equals AP at the maximum of AP, which comes earlier.

questions.s: In the law of variable proportions, the second stage, in which a rational producer operates, begins where
o: total product is at its maximum
marginal product is at its maximum
average product is at its maximum
questions.e: Stage II runs from the point where AP is highest (and equals MP) to the point where MP is zero. The maximum of MP lies in Stage I, and negative MP marks Stage III.

questions.s: If a firm doubles all its inputs and its output more than doubles, it is experiencing
questions.e: Returns to scale compare a proportional change in all inputs with the change in output; output rising by more than the input change is increasing returns. Diminishing returns refers to one variable factor with others fixed.

questions.s: Which cost stays the same whatever the level of output in the short run?
questions.e: Fixed costs, such as rent, must be paid even at zero output. Raw materials, daily wages and power for machines rise with output, so they are variable costs.

questions.s: A firm's total fixed cost is Rs 12,000. Its average fixed cost when it produces 400 units is
questions.e: AFC = TFC ÷ output = 12,000 ÷ 400 = Rs 30. AFC keeps falling as output rises because the same fixed cost is spread over more units.

questions.s: Total cost of producing 10 units is Rs 500 and of producing 11 units is Rs 560. What is the marginal cost of the 11th unit?
questions.e: MC = TC(11) − TC(10) = 560 − 500 = Rs 60. Rs 50 is the average cost of 10 units, and about Rs 51 is the average cost of 11 units.

questions.s: A firm's total cost is Rs 8,000 at an output of 100 units, of which Rs 3,000 is fixed. What is its average variable cost?
questions.e: TVC = TC − TFC = 8,000 − 3,000 = Rs 5,000, so AVC = 5,000 ÷ 100 = Rs 50. Rs 80 is average total cost and Rs 30 is average fixed cost.

questions.s: The marginal cost curve cuts the average cost curve
o: at the point where fixed cost is zero
where average cost is still falling steeply
at the highest point of the average cost curve
at the lowest point of the average cost curve
questions.e: When MC is below AC it pulls AC down, and when MC is above AC it pulls AC up, so MC must pass through the minimum of AC. The same is true for MC and AVC.

questions.s: The short-run average cost curve is usually U-shaped mainly because of
o: changes in the price of output
questions.e: At first, increasing returns to the variable factor lower average cost; later diminishing returns push it up, giving the U shape. In the long run the U shape is explained by economies and diseconomies of scale.

questions.s: Bulk buying of raw materials at a discount by a large firm is an example of
questions.e: Internal economies arise inside one firm as it grows, such as purchasing, technical and financial economies. External economies are shared by all firms in an industry, for example when an industry clusters in one city.

questions.s: Many textile firms setting up in Faisalabad leads to specialised training institutes and suppliers in the city, lowering costs for every firm. This is
o: increasing returns to a single factor
questions.e: Cost advantages that come from the growth of the whole industry in an area, rather than from one firm's own size, are external economies. An external diseconomy would raise costs, for example through congestion.

questions.s: Total revenue of a firm is equal to
questions.e: TR = P × Q. Price minus average cost gives profit per unit, not total revenue.

questions.s: A shop sells 8 units at Rs 50 each or 9 units at Rs 48 each. What is the marginal revenue of the 9th unit?
questions.e: TR(8) = 8 × 50 = Rs 400 and TR(9) = 9 × 48 = Rs 432, so MR = 432 − 400 = Rs 32. Rs 48 is the price (average revenue) of the 9th unit; MR is lower because the price cut applies to all units sold.

questions.s: Average revenue of a firm is the same as
questions.e: AR = TR ÷ Q = (P × Q) ÷ Q = P. So the demand curve facing a firm is also its average revenue curve.

questions.s: A firm maximises profit at the output where
o: average revenue equals average cost of production
average cost is at its minimum
total revenue is at its maximum
questions.e: If MR exceeds MC, producing one more unit adds to profit; if MC exceeds MR, it reduces profit. So profit is greatest where MR = MC, with MC rising. AR = AC only gives zero economic profit.

questions.s: Which is a feature of perfect competition?
o: Many sellers of slightly different products
Many sellers selling an identical product
One seller with no close substitutes
A few large firms that depend on each other
questions.e: Perfect competition has many buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and exit and perfect knowledge. A few interdependent firms is oligopoly, and differentiated products mark monopolistic competition.

questions.s: Under perfect competition, an individual firm's demand curve is
questions.e: Each firm is too small to affect price, so it can sell any quantity at the market price but nothing above it: its demand curve is perfectly elastic. A downward-sloping demand curve is faced by a monopolist.

questions.s: For a firm under perfect competition,
o: price, average revenue and marginal revenue are equal
marginal revenue is less than price
the firm can raise its price without losing any of its sales
average revenue falls as output rises
questions.e: Since every unit sells at the same market price, each extra unit adds exactly the price to revenue: P = AR = MR. MR below price happens only when a firm must cut price to sell more.

questions.s: In the long run, firms in a perfectly competitive industry earn
questions.e: Supernormal profits attract new firms, raising market supply and lowering price; losses drive firms out. With free entry and exit, price settles at minimum average cost and only normal profit remains.

questions.s: A perfectly competitive firm should shut down in the short run if the price falls below
questions.e: Below minimum AVC the firm cannot even cover its variable costs, so producing loses more than shutting down, where the loss is only fixed cost. Between AVC and ATC it keeps producing at a loss to cover part of its fixed cost.

questions.s: A market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes is called
questions.e: Monopoly means one seller. Duopoly has two sellers, oligopoly a few sellers, and monopsony means a single buyer.

questions.s: For a monopolist facing a downward-sloping demand curve, marginal revenue is
questions.e: To sell an extra unit the monopolist must lower the price on all units, so the addition to total revenue is below the new price. The MR curve therefore lies below the AR (demand) curve.

questions.s: Which of these can be a source of monopoly power?
o: Free entry of new firms into the market
A patent on a new medicine
Many small firms selling one product
questions.e: A patent legally stops others from producing the item, creating a barrier to entry. Free entry and many small firms are features of competitive markets, which remove monopoly power.

questions.s: A monopolist charges students a lower price than other customers for the same internet package. This is
questions.e: Price discrimination means charging different prices to different groups for the same product, for reasons not linked to cost. It needs separable markets with different elasticities; students usually have more elastic demand.

questions.s: Which market form has many sellers selling differentiated products, such as brands of shampoo?
questions.e: Monopolistic competition combines many sellers and free entry with product differentiation, so firms advertise and have a small degree of price control. Perfect competition has identical products.

questions.s: Under monopolistic competition, the demand curve facing a firm is
questions.e: Each firm has a slightly different product, so it can raise price a little without losing all its buyers, but close substitutes make demand quite elastic. A horizontal demand curve belongs to perfect competition.

questions.s: According to the marginal productivity theory, a firm employs workers up to the point where the wage equals
o: the cost of living of workers and their families
the total revenue of the firm
the marginal revenue product of labour
questions.e: Hiring one more worker adds MRP (MP × MR) to revenue and the wage to cost, so the firm keeps hiring until MRP = wage. Paying the cost of living is the subsistence theory of wages, an older idea.

questions.s: A worker's money wage rises by 10 % while prices rise by 15 %. His real wage has
questions.e: Real wage is what the money wage can buy. Prices rising faster than the money wage mean he can buy less, so his real wage falls by roughly 5 %.

questions.s: A machine operator earns Rs 60,000 a month, but his best alternative job would pay Rs 45,000. His economic rent is
questions.e: Transfer earnings are what is needed to keep a factor in its present use, here Rs 45,000. Economic rent is any earning above that: 60,000 − 45,000 = Rs 15,000. Rs 45,000 is the transfer earnings, not the rent.

questions.s: The extra earnings that a machine makes in the short run, before new machines can be built to compete, are called
questions.e: Marshall used quasi-rent for short-run surplus earnings of man-made factors whose supply is fixed for a time. They disappear in the long run as supply increases.

questions.s: In Keynes's liquidity preference theory, the rate of interest is
o: the price of land for a period
the reward for waiting, saving or abstinence from spending
the reward for parting with liquidity
questions.e: Keynes said people prefer to hold cash for transactions, precautionary and speculative motives; interest is paid to persuade them to give up that liquidity. The reward for abstinence is the classical view, and for uncertainty is profit.

questions.s: According to Frank Knight, profit is the reward for
o: working as a manager for a salary
bearing uncertainties that cannot be insured
supplying capital and loans to a business
questions.e: Knight separated insurable risks, which are a cost, from uninsurable uncertainty such as changes in demand; profit is the reward for bearing the latter. Supplying capital earns interest and managing earns wages.

questions.s: Normal profit is best described as
o: the total revenue of a firm
the minimum profit needed to keep an entrepreneur in the industry
questions.e: Normal profit is the opportunity cost of the entrepreneur and is counted as part of total cost. Profit above it is supernormal (abnormal) profit.

questions.s: A firm sells 500 units at Rs 40 each. Its total cost is Rs 15,000. What is its profit?
questions.e: TR = 500 × 40 = Rs 20,000. Profit = TR − TC = 20,000 − 15,000 = Rs 5,000. Rs 20,000 is total revenue, not profit.

questions.s: A firm's fixed cost is Rs 30,000, its variable cost is Rs 40 per unit and it sells each unit for Rs 100. How many units must it sell to break even?
questions.e: Each unit contributes 100 − 40 = Rs 60 towards fixed cost. Break-even output = 30,000 ÷ 60 = 500 units. 300 units uses the full price of Rs 100 and ignores variable cost.

questions.s: The cost of the owner's own time and building used in the business, which involves no cash payment, is called
questions.e: Implicit costs are the opportunity costs of self-owned resources; explicit costs are cash payments to outsiders, such as wages and rent paid. Economists count both, accountants only explicit costs.

questions.s: In the long run,
o: at least one factor of production stays fixed
all factors of production are variable
questions.e: The long run is a period long enough to change every input, including plant size. In the short run at least one factor, usually capital, is fixed.

questions.s: The long-run average cost curve is often called an envelope curve because it
o: shows only fixed costs of the firm
lies above every one of the short-run cost curves
touches a series of short-run average cost curves
questions.e: Each point on the LAC is the lowest cost of producing that output with the best plant size, so it is tangent to the SAC curves from below and wraps them like an envelope.

questions.s: A firm grows so large that managers lose control and communication slows down, raising average cost. This is
questions.e: Managerial problems in very large firms raise long-run average cost: internal diseconomies of scale. Economies of scale lower average cost as size grows.

questions.s: Which of the following is a variable cost for a bakery?
questions.e: Flour used rises with the number of loaves baked, so it is variable. Insurance, licence fees and loan interest must be paid whatever the output, so they are fixed.

questions.s: Compared with a perfectly competitive industry having the same costs, a monopolist usually
o: charges a lower price and produces more
charges the same price and produces more
charges a higher price and produces more
charges a higher price and produces less
questions.e: The monopolist sets output where MR = MC, and since MR is below price, this output is smaller than the competitive one where P = MC. With less output, the price on the demand curve is higher.

questions.s: In the kinked demand curve model of oligopoly, prices tend to be stable because rivals
o: match price rises but not price cuts
match price cuts but not price rises
never react to any price change
questions.e: If one firm cuts price, rivals follow to keep their share, so demand below the kink is inelastic; if it raises price, rivals do not follow, so demand above the kink is elastic. Either change hurts the firm, so prices stay sticky.

questions.s: A group of firms that agree to fix prices and share out the market is called
questions.e: A cartel is a formal agreement among oligopolists to restrict output and raise price, acting like a single monopolist. OPEC is a well-known example of a cartel among countries.

questions.s: A market with only one buyer of a product or factor is called
questions.e: Monopsony is a single buyer, for example a sugar mill that is the only buyer of cane in an area. Monopoly is a single seller, and oligopsony means a few buyers.

questions.s: Production in economics means
o: the selling of goods for profit
questions.e: Matter cannot be created; production adds utility to it by changing its form, place, time or ownership. Services such as teaching are also production.

questions.s: When a trader buys wheat at harvest and sells it some months later when it is scarce, he creates
questions.e: Storing a good until it is needed more adds time utility. Changing its form, such as turning wheat into flour, is form utility; moving it to where it is needed is place utility.

questions.s: A firm under perfect competition has the following at its profit-maximising output: price Rs 20, average total cost Rs 16 and output 1,000 units. Its supernormal profit is
questions.e: Profit per unit = P − ATC = 20 − 16 = Rs 4, so total supernormal profit = 4 × 1,000 = Rs 4,000. Rs 20,000 is total revenue and Rs 16,000 is total cost.

questions.s: The total cost of a firm is Rs 2,000 at zero output. This amount represents its
questions.e: At zero output no variable cost is incurred, so any cost that remains is fixed cost. Variable cost is zero when nothing is produced.

questions.s: Which statement about average fixed cost is correct?
o: It rises continuously as output rises
It stays constant at every output
It falls continuously as output rises
It is U-shaped like average variable cost
questions.e: Total fixed cost is constant, so spreading it over more units makes AFC fall without limit, giving a rectangular hyperbola. It is total fixed cost, not AFC, that stays constant.

questions.s: The use of more machines and fewer workers in production is called
questions.e: Capital-intensive methods use a high ratio of capital to labour, as in a modern car plant. Labour-intensive methods, common in handicrafts, use many workers and few machines.

questions.s: A firm's total cost function is TC = 100 + 5Q. What is the average total cost when Q = 20?
questions.e: TC at Q = 20 is 100 + 100 = Rs 200, so ATC = 200 ÷ 20 = Rs 10. Rs 5 is the marginal (and average variable) cost, and Rs 200 is total cost.

questions.s: The demand for a factor of production, such as labour, is a derived demand because
o: workers decide how much to work
it depends on demand for the goods it produces
its supply is fixed in the short run
it is fixed by the government's wage policy
questions.e: Firms want workers only for what they produce, so demand for labour rises and falls with demand for the final product. A fixed supply describes land, not the nature of factor demand.

questions.s: The main feature of oligopoly is that
o: one firm controls the whole market supply
many small firms sell an identical, standard product
a few large firms depend on each other's decisions
a single buyer faces many sellers
questions.e: With only a few sellers, each firm's price and output choice affects rivals, who react: this interdependence defines oligopoly. A single buyer facing many sellers is monopsony.

questions.s: In Ricardo's theory, rent arises on better land because
o: land differs in fertility and its supply is limited
governments tax the poorest land heavily
landlords hold monopoly power over all buyers of crops
farmers borrow money to buy land
questions.e: Ricardo saw rent as a differential surplus: superior land yields more than the marginal (no-rent) land at the same cost, and since good land is scarce, the surplus goes to its owner as rent.

questions.s: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures the market value of
o: all goods sold in a country, including second-hand goods, in a year
all final goods and services produced within a country in a year
all intermediate goods used by the country's firms
all goods and services produced by a country's citizens abroad
questions.e: GDP counts final output produced inside the country's borders, by residents or foreigners, in a period. Output by citizens abroad is added for GNP, and second-hand sales and intermediate goods are excluded to avoid counting the same output twice.

questions.s: GNP is obtained from GDP by
o: subtracting transfer payments made by the government
adding net factor income from abroad
questions.e: GNP = GDP + (factor income earned abroad by residents − factor income paid to foreigners). Subtracting depreciation turns gross into net values, giving NDP or NNP.

questions.s: A country's GDP is Rs 900 billion. Its residents earn Rs 60 billion abroad and foreigners earn Rs 20 billion in the country. Its GNP is
questions.e: Net factor income from abroad = 60 − 20 = Rs 40 billion, so GNP = 900 + 40 = Rs 940 billion. Rs 960 billion adds the 60 but forgets to subtract the 20 paid out.

questions.s: Net National Product at market price is GNP minus
questions.e: Depreciation (capital consumption) is the value of capital worn out in producing output; deducting it from GNP gives NNP. Removing indirect taxes and adding subsidies converts market price to factor cost.

questions.s: NNP at market price is Rs 800 billion, indirect taxes are Rs 90 billion and subsidies are Rs 30 billion. National income (NNP at factor cost) is
questions.e: NNP at factor cost = NNP at market price − indirect taxes + subsidies = 800 − 90 + 30 = Rs 740 billion. Adding taxes and subtracting subsidies, the reverse step, gives Rs 860 billion.

questions.s: Which of the following is included in GDP?
o: Wages paid to a government schoolteacher
Money a student receives from her father
A pension paid to a retired soldier
questions.e: A teacher's wage is payment for a service produced in the year. Pensions and gifts are transfer payments with no current output in return, and a used car was counted when it was first made.

questions.s: The problem of double counting in national income accounts is avoided by
o: counting only final goods or the value added at each stage
counting only goods sold to the government
counting the output of every firm in full
excluding all services from the accounts
questions.e: If the sale of wheat, flour and bread were all added, the wheat would be counted three times. Adding only the final product, or the value added at each stage, counts it once.

questions.s: A farmer sells wheat to a miller for Rs 500, the miller sells flour to a baker for Rs 800 and the baker sells bread for Rs 1,200. The total value added is
questions.e: Value added = 500 (farmer) + 300 (miller) + 400 (baker) = Rs 1,200, the same as the value of the final good. Rs 2,500 adds all sales and counts the wheat and flour more than once.

questions.s: Which method measures national income by adding wages, rent, interest and profit?
questions.e: The income method sums factor incomes earned in production. The expenditure method adds C + I + G + (X − M), and the output or value added method sums the value of production in each sector.

questions.s: Under the expenditure method, GDP equals
questions.e: Spending on domestic output comes from consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports. Wages, rent, interest and profit (W + R + I + P) belong to the income method.

questions.s: Real GDP differs from nominal GDP because real GDP
o: is measured at the prices of a base year
is measured at current market prices
includes the value of exports and imports
excludes the output of the government
questions.e: Valuing output at constant base-year prices removes the effect of inflation, so real GDP changes only when actual quantities change. Nominal GDP uses current prices.

questions.s: Nominal GDP is Rs 1,500 billion and the GDP deflator is 125 (base year = 100). Real GDP is
questions.e: Real GDP = nominal GDP × 100 ÷ deflator = 1,500 × 100 ÷ 125 = Rs 1,200 billion. Multiplying by 1.25 instead of dividing gives Rs 1,875 billion.

questions.s: Per capita income of a country is
o: income of each worker in the government
total income of the richest families
questions.e: Per capita income is the average income per person, found by dividing national income by the total population. It is a rough indicator of living standards but hides inequality.

questions.s: Disposable personal income is
o: personal income minus personal direct taxes
personal income plus all transfer payments received
questions.e: Disposable income is what households can actually spend or save after paying income tax and other personal direct taxes. Transfer payments are already part of personal income.

questions.s: Why is the work of a housewife caring for her own family not included in GDP?
o: It is done only part of the time, not full-time
It is taxed separately by the state
It is not sold for a price in the market
It produces no utility for anyone
questions.e: National accounts record mainly market transactions, so unpaid household work is left out even though it is valuable. The same service bought from a paid cook would be counted.

questions.s: According to Keynes, as income rises, consumption
o: rises, but by less than the rise in income
rises by more than the rise in income
remains exactly the same as before
falls by the same amount as income rises
questions.e: Keynes's psychological law of consumption says people spend part of any increase in income and save the rest, so 0 < MPC < 1.

questions.s: When national income rises from Rs 500 billion to Rs 600 billion, consumption rises from Rs 400 billion to Rs 480 billion. The marginal propensity to consume is
questions.e: MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔY = 80 ÷ 100 = 0.8. 0.2 is the MPS, and 0.96 wrongly divides the new consumption by the old income (480 ÷ 500).

questions.s: If the marginal propensity to consume is 0.75, the marginal propensity to save is
questions.e: Each extra rupee of income is either consumed or saved, so MPC + MPS = 1 and MPS = 1 − 0.75 = 0.25. 4 is the multiplier, 1 ÷ 0.25.

questions.s: A household earns Rs 50,000 a month and spends Rs 40,000. Its average propensity to save is
questions.e: Saving = 50,000 − 40,000 = Rs 10,000, so APS = S ÷ Y = 10,000 ÷ 50,000 = 0.2. 0.8 is the APC, and 0.25 is saving divided by consumption.

questions.s: If the MPC is 0.8, the value of the investment multiplier is
questions.e: Multiplier k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5. Using 1 ÷ MPC gives 1.25, a common slip.

questions.s: In a closed economy with no government, the MPC is 0.75. If investment rises by Rs 20 billion, national income will rise by
questions.e: k = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.75) = 4, so ΔY = 4 × 20 = Rs 80 billion. Rs 15 billion is only the first round of extra consumption, 0.75 × 20.

questions.s: An increase in investment of Rs 10 billion raises national income by Rs 50 billion. What is the marginal propensity to save?
questions.e: Multiplier = 50 ÷ 10 = 5 = 1 ÷ MPS, so MPS = 0.2 and MPC = 0.8. 0.8 is the MPC, and 5 is the multiplier itself.

questions.s: The size of the multiplier is larger when
o: more of each extra rupee of income is spent on imports
people hoard more of their extra income
the marginal propensity to save is higher
the marginal propensity to consume is higher
questions.e: k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC): the more of each extra rupee is spent at home, the more rounds of spending follow. Saving, hoarding and imports are leakages that make the multiplier smaller.

questions.s: The paradox of thrift states that if all households try to save more,
o: total saving may not rise because income falls
total saving always rises by the full amount planned
questions.e: Higher saving means lower consumption and less demand, so output and income fall through the multiplier; with lower income, total saving may end up no higher. What is wise for one household can harm the whole economy.

questions.s: At the break-even level of income on a consumption function,
o: consumption equals income and saving is zero
saving is at its highest possible level
questions.e: Break-even income is where the consumption line crosses the 45° line, so C = Y and S = 0. Below it saving is negative (dissaving); above it saving is positive.

questions.s: The consumption function is C = 50 + 0.6Y. At what level of income is saving zero?
questions.e: Saving is zero where C = Y: Y = 50 + 0.6Y, so 0.4Y = 50 and Y = 125. 83.3 comes from dividing 50 by 0.6, the MPC, instead of by the MPS.

questions.s: Investment in economics means
o: spending on new capital goods such as machines and buildings
keeping money in a savings account
buying gold to hold as savings
buying shares of an existing company
questions.e: Economic investment adds to the stock of real capital. Buying existing shares or gold only transfers ownership of assets; it is financial investment, not addition to capital.

questions.s: According to Keynes, a firm will invest in a new project when
o: consumption is falling across the economy
the government lowers income tax rates
the marginal efficiency of capital exceeds the rate of interest
the rate of interest exceeds the marginal efficiency of capital
questions.e: MEC is the expected rate of return on new capital. If it is higher than the cost of borrowing, the investment is profitable. A higher interest rate than MEC makes the project a loss.

questions.s: Investment that does not depend on the level of income, such as government spending on a new dam, is called
questions.e: Autonomous investment is independent of income and profit; it is driven by long-term factors such as technology or public policy. Induced investment rises with income.

questions.s: The accelerator principle states that investment depends on
o: the level of saving of households
the rate of change of output or demand
the level of the rate of interest only
questions.e: If firms need a fixed amount of capital per unit of output, net investment is needed only when output grows, so investment depends on changes in demand. The multiplier works the other way, from investment to income.

questions.s: A worker who has left one job and is searching for a better one is in
questions.e: Frictional unemployment is the short-term unemployment of people moving between jobs or entering the labour market. Structural unemployment results from a mismatch of skills after changes in the economy.

questions.s: Workers in the handloom industry lose their jobs permanently after power looms replace hand looms. This is
questions.e: A lasting change in technology or the pattern of demand that makes certain skills obsolete causes structural unemployment. Frictional unemployment is short and occurs while people move between jobs.

questions.s: Unemployment caused by a general fall in aggregate demand during a recession is called
questions.e: Cyclical (demand-deficient) unemployment rises in the downswing of the business cycle and falls in recovery. Keynes argued it can be cured by raising aggregate demand.

questions.s: Eight members of a family work on a small farm that four people could manage with the same output. The extra four are in
questions.e: Disguised unemployment means people appear employed, but their marginal product is zero: removing them would not reduce output. It is common in the farm sector of developing countries.

questions.s: Sugar mill workers who are idle each year after the crushing season ends face
questions.e: Work that depends on the season, such as crushing cane or harvesting, leaves workers idle for part of the year. This is seasonal unemployment and recurs regularly.

questions.s: Say's law of markets, the basis of the classical theory of employment, states that
questions.e: J. B. Say argued that producing goods generates the income needed to buy them, so general overproduction and lasting unemployment cannot occur. Keynes rejected this view.

questions.s: In Keynes's theory, the level of employment in the short run is determined by
questions.e: Keynes held that firms produce, and hire, only as much as they expect to sell, so employment depends on effective demand (aggregate demand where it equals aggregate supply). Classical economists relied on flexible wages.

questions.s: Inflation means
o: a rise in the value of money
a fall in the general price level
a rise in the price of one particular good or service
a sustained rise in the general price level
questions.e: Inflation is a continuing rise in the average level of prices, so the value (purchasing power) of money falls. A fall in the general price level is deflation.

questions.s: Inflation that occurs because aggregate demand exceeds the economy's capacity to produce is called
questions.e: Demand-pull inflation is 'too much money chasing too few goods'. Cost-push inflation starts from rising costs such as wages or oil prices that firms pass on to buyers.

questions.s: A sharp rise in the world price of oil raises transport and production costs and then prices across the economy. This is
questions.e: Higher input costs shift aggregate supply to the left, pushing the price level up. Demand-pull inflation starts from spending, not from costs.

questions.s: Who generally loses from unexpected inflation?
o: People living on a fixed money income
Holders of goods whose prices rise
Firms whose selling prices rise first
questions.e: A fixed money income buys less as prices rise. Borrowers gain because they repay loans in money that is worth less, and holders of rising-price goods also gain.

questions.s: A situation in which high inflation exists together with high unemployment and slow growth is called
questions.e: Stagflation combines stagnation and inflation, often after a supply shock such as an oil price rise. Hyperinflation is extremely rapid inflation, and reflation is a deliberate policy to raise demand after a slump.

questions.s: A consumer price index rises from 160 to 176 in a year. The rate of inflation is
questions.e: Inflation = (176 − 160) ÷ 160 × 100 = 16 ÷ 160 × 100 = 10 %. 16 % is the change in index points, not the percentage change, and 9.1 % divides by the new value.

questions.s: A price index uses a base year value of 100. If the index is 250 today, the value of money compared with the base year is
questions.e: The value of money moves inversely with the price level: 100 ÷ 250 = 0.4, so a rupee buys 40 % of what it bought in the base year. 60 % is the fall in value, not what remains.

questions.s: Deflation is
o: a fall in a country's exchange rate
a slower rate of inflation than in the previous year
a sustained fall in the general price level
a fall in the price of one good
questions.e: Deflation means prices on average are falling. A slowing of the inflation rate while prices still rise is called disinflation.

questions.s: The phase of a business cycle in which output and employment are at their highest is
questions.e: A cycle moves through recovery, boom (peak), recession and trough. At the peak output, employment and often prices are at their highest before the downswing starts.

questions.s: During a recession, which is most likely?
o: Demand for labour keeps rising sharply
Unemployment falls and business profits rise
Prices rise faster than in a boom
Unemployment rises and business profits fall
questions.e: A recession is a fall in real output; firms cut production and hire less, so unemployment rises and profits fall. Falling unemployment and rising profits belong to the recovery and boom.

questions.s: Fiscal policy refers to the use of
o: price controls on essential goods only
government spending and taxation to influence the economy
interest rates and the money supply by the central bank
exchange rates to control imports and exports
questions.e: Fiscal policy is run by the government through its budget. Changing interest rates and money supply is monetary policy, run by the central bank.

questions.s: To reduce unemployment during a recession, the government should follow
o: a balanced budget with spending cuts
a policy of higher income tax rates
questions.e: Higher government spending or lower taxes raise aggregate demand, output and employment through the multiplier. Contractionary policy, such as higher taxes, is used to cool inflation.

questions.s: A budget deficit occurs when
o: the central bank prints less money
imports of a country exceed its exports
questions.e: A deficit is a shortfall of revenue relative to spending in a year, usually met by borrowing. An excess of imports over exports is a trade deficit, a separate idea.

questions.s: When the government raises spending and taxes by the same amount, Rs 10 billion, the simple Keynesian model predicts that national income will
questions.e: The balanced budget multiplier is 1: the spending multiplier 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) exceeds the tax multiplier MPC ÷ (1 − MPC) by exactly 1, so income rises by the amount of the spending. Assuming the two cancel gives no change.

questions.s: Government borrowing to finance a deficit raises interest rates and reduces private investment. This effect is called
questions.e: Crowding out means public spending financed by borrowing displaces some private investment, which weakens the effect of fiscal expansion. Fiscal drag is when inflation pushes taxpayers into higher tax brackets.

questions.s: Progressive income tax and unemployment benefits are called automatic stabilisers because they
o: keep the government's budget exactly balanced in every year
fix the price level at a constant value
reduce swings in demand without new government decisions
are changed by parliament every month
questions.e: In a boom, tax receipts rise and benefit payments fall, restraining demand; in a slump the reverse happens. This happens automatically, without any new policy decision.

questions.s: If MPC is 0.9 and the government raises its spending by Rs 5 billion, the rise in national income will be
questions.e: k = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.9) = 10, so ΔY = 10 × 5 = Rs 50 billion. Rs 4.5 billion is only the first round of extra spending, and Rs 5.6 billion uses 1 ÷ MPC.

questions.s: Aggregate demand in an economy is the total
o: output a country produces in one year
planned spending on goods and services at each price level
questions.e: Aggregate demand is the sum C + I + G + (X − M) that all buyers plan to spend at each price level. Total output is aggregate supply.

questions.s: Transfer payments, such as old-age pensions, are
o: payments made without any current goods or services in return
payments made to factors of production
payments for imported goods and services
questions.e: Transfers only redistribute income, so they are left out of GDP. Wages of government employees pay for a current service and are included.

questions.s: If the consumption function is C = 100 + 0.8Y, the average propensity to consume at an income of 1,000 is
questions.e: At Y = 1,000, C = 100 + 800 = 900, so APC = 900 ÷ 1,000 = 0.9. 0.8 is the MPC, the slope of the function; APC is higher because of the autonomous 100.

questions.s: A rise in the general price level that is extremely rapid, such as prices doubling every few weeks, is called
questions.e: Hyperinflation destroys confidence in money, so people switch to barter or foreign currency. Creeping inflation is a slow, mild rise in prices of a few per cent a year.

questions.s: Which statement about the GDP deflator is correct?
o: It equals nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100
It measures only the prices of consumer goods
It equals real GDP divided by nominal GDP, times 100
It is always equal to the consumer price index
questions.e: The deflator = nominal GDP ÷ real GDP × 100 and covers all goods in GDP, including capital goods. The CPI covers only a fixed basket of consumer goods, so the two usually differ.

questions.s: Leakages from the circular flow of income include
questions.e: Saving, taxes and imports withdraw income from the flow of spending on domestic output. Investment, government spending and exports are injections that add to it.

questions.s: In a two-sector Keynesian model, equilibrium national income is reached when
o: investment is at its maximum level
questions.e: Equilibrium requires aggregate demand C + I to equal output Y; since Y = C + S, this means planned S = planned I. If I exceeds S, income rises; if S exceeds I, income falls.

questions.s: The study of the economy as a whole, including national income, inflation and unemployment, is called
questions.e: Macroeconomics deals with aggregates. Microeconomics studies individual households, firms and markets, as in consumer theory.

questions.s: The main difficulty of a barter system is the need for
o: a central bank to issue notes
a fixed rate of interest on loans
questions.e: In barter, each trader must find someone who both has what he wants and wants what he has. Money removes this need by acting as a medium of exchange.

questions.s: When the prices of all goods are expressed in rupees, money is serving as
o: a store of value over time
a medium of exchange in day-to-day trade
a unit of account (measure of value)
questions.e: Using money as a common yardstick to state and compare the values of goods is its function as a unit of account. Being accepted in payment is its function as a medium of exchange.

questions.s: Money's function as a standard of deferred payments means it is used to
o: measure the value of the goods that are sold today
settle payments that are due in the future
buy goods directly in the market
questions.e: Loans, instalments and salaries agreed now but paid later are stated in money, so it serves as a standard for deferred payments. This works well only when the value of money is fairly stable.

questions.s: Saving part of one's income as money to spend next year uses money as
questions.e: Money lets people hold purchasing power over time, unlike perishable goods. High inflation weakens this function because money loses value while it is held.

questions.s: Paper currency that is money because the government declares it so, and is not backed by gold, is called
questions.e: Fiat money has value by government order (fiat) and people's confidence, not because of the material it is made of. Commodity money, such as gold coins, has value as a good in itself.

questions.s: Money that must be accepted by law in settlement of a debt is called
questions.e: Legal tender cannot lawfully be refused in payment of a debt; currency notes and coins issued by the authorities are legal tender. Cheques are optional money because a creditor may refuse them.

questions.s: Assets such as savings deposits and treasury bills, which can quickly be turned into cash but are not themselves a medium of exchange, are called
questions.e: Near money is highly liquid but cannot be spent directly; it must first be converted into cash or a current-account balance. Legal tender is money that must be accepted in payment.

questions.s: Gresham's law states that
o: good money drives bad money out of circulation
the supply of money creates its own demand
the value of money rises as prices rise
bad money drives good money out of circulation
questions.e: When two kinds of money with the same face value circulate, people hoard or melt the one of higher intrinsic value and spend the poorer one, so the 'bad' money remains in use.

questions.s: In Fisher's quantity theory of money, MV = PT, the letter V stands for
o: the velocity of circulation of money
the value of the currency in foreign markets
questions.e: V is the average number of times each unit of money changes hands in a period. T is the volume of transactions, P the price level and M the money supply.

questions.s: According to the simple quantity theory of money, with V and T constant, doubling the money supply will
questions.e: If MV = PT with V and T fixed, P moves in proportion to M. The value of money, 1 ÷ P, would halve.

questions.s: In an economy, M = Rs 500 billion, V = 6 and T = 1,000 billion units of transactions. Using MV = PT, the price level P is
questions.e: P = MV ÷ T = (500 × 6) ÷ 1,000 = 3,000 ÷ 1,000 = 3. Dividing T by MV gives 0.33, the inverse.

questions.s: The value of money means
o: the face value printed on a currency note or coin by the state
the amount of goods and services a unit of money can buy
the rate of interest paid on bank deposits
the cost of printing a currency note
questions.e: The value of money is its purchasing power, which falls when the general price level rises. The printed face value stays the same whatever the prices.

questions.s: Which of the following is a primary function of a commercial bank?
o: Issuing currency notes for the country
Acting as banker to the government
questions.e: Commercial banks earn mainly by accepting deposits and lending them out. Issuing notes, acting as the government's banker and controlling credit are functions of the central bank.

questions.s: Which deposit can be withdrawn at any time by cheque and usually pays no interest?
questions.e: Current accounts suit businesses that make frequent payments, so they offer full withdrawal by cheque but little or no interest. Fixed deposits pay higher interest but are locked for a set period.

questions.s: A bank receives a new cash deposit of Rs 10,000. If the required reserve ratio is 20 % and banks lend out all excess reserves, the maximum total deposits created in the banking system are
questions.e: Credit multiplier = 1 ÷ reserve ratio = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5, so total deposits = 5 × 10,000 = Rs 50,000. Rs 8,000 is only the first loan the bank can make.

questions.s: A commercial bank faces a conflict between liquidity and profitability because
o: the most liquid assets earn the highest returns
its depositors never withdraw their money
the central bank fixes its profits every year
the most liquid assets earn the lowest returns
questions.e: Cash is perfectly liquid but earns nothing, while long-term loans earn more but cannot be turned into cash quickly. A bank must balance the two to meet withdrawals and still make a profit.

questions.s: The central bank of Pakistan is
questions.e: The State Bank of Pakistan is the country's central bank: it issues notes, acts as banker to the government and to banks, and runs monetary policy. The National Bank of Pakistan is a commercial bank, though it acts as the SBP's agent in some places.

questions.s: Which is a function of a central bank but not of a commercial bank?
o: Providing lockers for customers' gold and valuables
Giving loans to traders and farmers
questions.e: The central bank has the monopoly of note issue. Deposits, loans and lockers are ordinary services provided by commercial banks.

questions.s: To control inflation, a central bank is most likely to
o: lower the interest rate on loans to banks
buy government securities in the open market
questions.e: A higher policy rate makes borrowing dearer, reduces credit and spending, and so lowers demand-pull inflation. Lowering reserve ratios or buying securities would expand money supply, the opposite effect.

questions.s: When the central bank sells government securities in the open market,
o: bank reserves and the money supply rise
bank reserves and the money supply fall
questions.e: Buyers pay for the securities from their bank deposits, draining reserves from the banking system, so banks must cut lending and the money supply falls. Buying securities injects reserves instead.

questions.s: Which is a selective (qualitative) tool of credit control?
o: Changing the bank rate for all lending
Fixing margin requirements on loans against particular goods
Changing the cash reserve ratio required of all banks alike
Open market operations in government securities
questions.e: Selective tools direct credit to or away from particular uses, for example higher margins on loans against stocks of a scarce commodity. Bank rate, CRR and open market operations affect the total volume of credit.

questions.s: A central bank persuading commercial banks, through meetings and advice, to follow its policy is called
questions.e: Moral suasion uses persuasion rather than legal force. Direct action means penalties against banks that do not follow instructions, and credit rationing sets limits on loans.

questions.s: An expansionary (easy) monetary policy is designed to
o: raise taxes and cut government spending
fix the exchange rate of the currency
reduce the money supply and raise interest rates
increase money supply and lower interest rates
questions.e: Easy money policy encourages borrowing, investment and spending, so it is used in a recession. Raising taxes and cutting spending is contractionary fiscal policy, not monetary policy.

questions.s: A tax whose burden cannot be shifted to someone else, such as income tax, is called
questions.e: The impact and incidence of a direct tax fall on the same person. Indirect taxes, such as sales tax and excise duties, are paid by sellers but can be passed on to buyers through higher prices.

questions.s: Which of the following is an indirect tax?
questions.e: Sales tax is collected from sellers but its burden passes to buyers in the price. Income, wealth and corporate taxes are paid directly by the person or company on whom they are levied.

questions.s: A tax system in which the rate of tax rises as income rises is called
questions.e: Under progressive taxation richer people pay a larger percentage of their income. A proportional tax charges the same rate at every income, and a regressive tax takes a larger share from the poor.

questions.s: Ali earns Rs 20,000 and Sara earns Rs 80,000 a month. Both pay the same sales tax of Rs 2,000 on their monthly purchases. As a share of income, this tax is
questions.e: The tax takes 10 % of Ali's income but only 2.5 % of Sara's, so the poorer person pays a larger share: a regressive tax. A proportional tax would take the same percentage from both.

questions.s: Adam Smith's canon of certainty says that
o: the amount, time and manner of paying a tax should be clear
taxes should be paid at a convenient time
taxes should be in proportion to each person's ability to pay
taxes should cost little to collect
questions.e: Certainty means the taxpayer knows what, when and how to pay. Ability to pay is the canon of equality, low collection cost is economy, and a suitable time to pay is convenience.

questions.s: A tax of Rs 5 per unit is placed on a good with perfectly elastic demand. The incidence of the tax falls
questions.e: With perfectly elastic demand, buyers will not pay any higher price, so sellers cannot pass on the tax and must bear it themselves. With perfectly inelastic demand, consumers would bear it all.

questions.s: Money borrowed by a government from its own citizens and banks is called
questions.e: Internal debt is owed to lenders within the country; external debt is owed to foreign governments, institutions or lenders and must usually be repaid in foreign currency.

questions.s: The theory of comparative advantage was developed by
questions.e: Ricardo showed that trade benefits both countries even if one is better at producing everything, as long as their opportunity costs differ. Adam Smith gave the earlier theory of absolute advantage.

questions.s: In Country A, one worker-day produces 10 metres of cloth or 5 kg of rice. In Country B, one worker-day produces 6 metres of cloth or 4 kg of rice. Which pattern of specialisation follows comparative advantage?
o: A makes both goods and B makes neither
A makes rice and B makes cloth
A makes cloth and B makes rice
questions.e: Opportunity cost of 1 kg rice: in A, 2 m of cloth; in B, 1.5 m. B gives up less cloth per kg of rice, so B has comparative advantage in rice and A in cloth. A's absolute advantage in both goods does not rule out gains from trade.

questions.s: A country has a comparative advantage in a good when it can produce it
o: with more output per worker in every good it makes
at a lower opportunity cost than other countries
at a higher price than other countries
with more workers than other countries
questions.e: Comparative advantage depends on what must be given up to produce the good. Producing more of every good per worker is absolute advantage, which is not needed for trade to be useful.

questions.s: A country's export price index rises from 100 to 120 while its import price index rises from 100 to 150. Its terms of trade index becomes
questions.e: Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100 = 120 ÷ 150 × 100 = 80. Below 100 means each unit of exports now buys fewer imports: the terms of trade have worsened. 125 is the inverse ratio.

questions.s: An improvement in a country's terms of trade means that
o: the balance of payments is now in surplus
a given quantity of exports buys more imports
the country now exports a larger quantity of goods than before
the country's imports have become dearer
